card_title: Same molecule, a very different idea
card_summary: Why a tiny dose of a decades-old medicine is a different conversation from the standard one.
headline: Same molecule. A *very* different idea.
lede: Standard naltrexone is a {{dose_standard_value}} daily tablet. Low-dose naltrexone, as studied, uses a small fraction of that. Here's why researchers think the size of the dose may change what it does, and what's still an open question.
recognition: Maybe a friend mentioned LDN, or you saw it in a forum thread. Then you looked it up and found a medicine best known at a much higher dose, for a very different purpose. Both of those things are true.
reframe: LDN is naltrexone at doses studied around {{dose_low_range}} a day, compared with the {{dose_standard_value}} tablet the FDA approved. Your clinician sets your strength. Researchers think a dose this small may act differently: a short, light touch on the same receptors. The leading theory is that your body responds to the touch.
viz_title: A brief block, then a response
viz_intro: Each lane follows one dose across a day. The plum band shows how long opioid receptors stay occupied. The gold dotted line is the leading theory of what your body does next.
viz_alt: Two timelines over 24 hours. Standard-dose naltrexone occupies opioid receptors all day. Low-dose naltrexone occupies them briefly, then a dotted line rises to show the theorized increase in the body's own signaling.
viz_caption: Illustration, not measured data. Band lengths show the idea, not exact hours, and the doses are the label dose and the studied range, not your dose. For scale: naltrexone itself has a half-life of about 4 hours, and its main active by-product about 13 hours.

viz_legend.legend_text: Solid edge: naltrexone blocks opioid receptors. Established, from the FDA label.
Dotted line: the rebound idea. A leading theory, mostly supported by animal research.

viz_scrub_prompt: Drag the slider to see what each dose is doing at that hour.

viz_scrub_states.state_text: Hour 0. The dose is taken and naltrexone reaches opioid receptors.
Early hours. Both doses occupy the receptors. The low dose is already fading.
Midday. The standard dose is still blocking. The low-dose block has lifted, and the theory says your body has turned its own signaling up in response.
Late day. Standard dose: still on duty. Low dose: the receptors are open, and any rebound in your own endorphins would be doing the work.

mechanism_title: Two theories, both still being tested
mechanism_intro: Nobody has fully pinned down how LDN works. These are the two explanations researchers take most seriously, followed by an honest read of the human data.

mechanism_steps.step_body: A brief block on opioid receptors may prompt your body to make more of its own endorphins and add more receptors. Over a full day, the net effect could be more of your own signaling, not less. Most of the support for this comes from animal and cell research.

Separately from opioid receptors, naltrexone appears to quiet a receptor called TLR4 on microglia, the resident immune cells of the brain and spinal cord. In lab work, a mirror-image form of naltrexone that doesn't touch opioid receptors still blocked TLR4. Researchers note the data don't fit this explanation perfectly.

mechanism_steps.step_title: What the human studies show so far
mechanism_steps.step_body: Most human studies of LDN have been small, with few repeats. A 2026 review of 105 studies, 15 of them randomized trials, found it was generally well tolerated but that the evidence lacks methodological strength. Early positive results from uncontrolled studies were rarely repeated in placebo-controlled trials. That's the honest state of the science, and it's why a clinician decides whether it's worth trying for you.

notice_intro: Every member is different. This is what studies have measured, not a promise.

notice_items.notice_text: Some people notice vivid dreams or lighter sleep early on. In small studies these were mostly mild and passed.
Studies have followed LDN for 8 to 12 weeks. Your clinician will tell you when to check in on how it's going.
Your clinician may adjust your strength or the time of day you take it. Tell them about any sleep changes.

route_intro: A capsule, compounded for you, on the schedule your clinician sets.
route_figure_label: Figure showing an oral capsule route from the mouth to the gut, with opioid receptors in the brain and spinal cord.

route_points.point_label: Opioid receptors in the brain and spinal cord

route_steps.route_text: You take one capsule a day, at the strength and time your clinician sets.
Naltrexone itself clears quickly, with a half-life of about 4 hours. Its main active by-product lasts about 13 hours.
No FDA-approved low-dose product exists, so a pharmacy compounds your capsules from naltrexone. This is an off-label use your clinician prescribes for you.

cautions_intro: Your clinician screens for these during your intake. Read them anyway.

not_for_you_if.item_text: You take any opioid, including prescription pain medicine, methadone or buprenorphine. Naltrexone blocks opioids and can bring on withdrawal.
You have acute hepatitis or liver failure. The naltrexone label lists both as reasons not to use it.

what_to_watch.item_text: Sleep changes or vivid dreams, especially in the first weeks.
Nausea, especially in the first few nights.
If you might need opioid pain relief, for example before a procedure, tell your clinician and care team that you take naltrexone.

cadence_intro: Your plan as it's set up today.
cta_note: A licensed clinician reviews your health history and decides whether LDN is appropriate for you. If it's prescribed, they choose your strength.
footer_note: Educational content for Equilibria members. It isn't medical advice. LDN is an off-label use of naltrexone, compounded by a pharmacy and prescribed only after a clinician's review.
